opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've spent a lot of time on, because there's a tempting assumption that cooperation is just good, and therefore more cooperative capability must be good. I don't think that holds automatically.

The way I'd frame it: cooperative skill is a capability like any other. It lets agents find and realize mutually beneficial outcomes. The key question is always "cooperation among whom, and at whose expense?" Cartels are cooperation. Collusion between firms to fix prices is cooperation. Coalitions that exclude or exploit outsiders are cooperation. So when we ask whether boosting cooperative competence across AI systems is beneficial, we have to look at who gains the ability to coordinate, and what happens to the people outside that circle.

A few considerations I'd weigh.

First, is the cooperative capability broadly distributed or concentrated? If many actors, including less powerful ones, get better at bargaining, communicating, making credible commitments, and building trust, that tends to expand the pie and make the overall system more stable. If it mostly goes to a narrow set of already powerful actors, it can entrench them and make it easier to coordinate against everyone else.

Second, does it differentially help the welfare-improving kinds of cooperation? Some skills, like understanding others' preferences, clear communication, and identifying win-win deals, mostly reduce bargaining failures and conflict. Others, like strong commitment ability, are double-edged: they can enable peace agreements, but also credible threats and coercion. So you want to be somewhat surgical about which components you push on.

Third, what does it do to humans' place in the loop? A world where AI systems get very good at cooperating with each other, but not necessarily with us or on our behalf, could be one where humans gradually lose bargaining power and oversight. AI-to-AI coordination that isn't anchored to human interests is a real risk, including the scenario of AI systems colluding in ways that undermine monitoring or safety mechanisms.

Fourth, what are the institutions around it? Cooperative skill in a world with good norms, transparency, and accountability is much more likely to be channeled toward public goods. The same skill in a lawless environment can just make defection and exploitation more efficient.

So my overall view is that, on balance, I'm optimistic that much of cooperative intelligence is socially beneficial, because so many of humanity's biggest problems, from war to climate to managing AI itself, are fundamentally cooperation failures. But that optimism is conditional. The research agenda shouldn't just be "make AI more cooperative." It should be "identify the forms of cooperative capability that are most robustly prosocial, distribute them widely, keep humans meaningfully empowered, and build the institutions that keep cooperation from becoming collusion."

r001.rationale: It describes cooperative skill as a capability that can enable mutually beneficial outcomes or harmful collusion, coercion, and exclusion.

r002.rationale: It says broadly distributed cooperative skills tend to expand the pie and concludes that, on balance, much of cooperative intelligence is socially beneficial, while making that optimism conditional.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we spent a lot of time on when we were writing the "Open Problems in Cooperative AI" paper, and I think it's genuinely one of the more subtle issues in the area. Because at first glance, "cooperation" sounds unambiguously good. Who could be against more cooperation? But if you think about it for a minute, you realise that cooperation is often a local phenomenon. Two agents cooperating with each other can be doing so at the expense of a third party. Cartels cooperate. Colluding firms cooperate. Criminal organisations are, in a sense, quite cooperative internally.

So the framing I find most useful is to ask: cooperation among whom, and against whom, or affecting whom? When we talk about increasing cooperative skill, we're usually talking about some set of capabilities — the ability to understand other agents' goals and beliefs, the ability to communicate credibly, the ability to make and keep commitments, the ability to build institutions that sustain cooperation over time. And each of those capabilities can be deployed in ways that are socially beneficial or socially harmful, depending on the structure of the situation.

The way I'd try to assess the net effect is to think about the structure of the externalities. If you have a world in which the dominant failure mode is that agents fail to cooperate when it would be in everyone's interest — Prisoner's Dilemma-type situations, coordination failures, bargaining breakdowns — then improving cooperative capabilities is likely to be very beneficial. A lot of the biggest problems facing humanity look like this: climate change, arms races, pandemic preparedness. Those are cases where everyone would be better off if we could coordinate, and we fail to do so because of commitment problems or trust problems or communication problems.

On the other hand, there are situations where the thing standing between some group and a harmful outcome is precisely their inability to cooperate. So price-fixing requires firms to coordinate, and the fact that it's hard for them to coordinate secretly is part of what protects consumers. Or a coup requires some group of elites to coordinate against the rest of society. So if you just hand out cooperative capabilities uniformly, you're also making those kinds of harmful coalitions easier to form.

What I'd say is that there are a few features that push me toward thinking that, on balance, increasing cooperative capability tends to be good. One is that the largest-scale coalitions — the ones that include all of humanity, or the ones that include the broadest set of stakeholders — are often the ones that are hardest to form, because they involve the most parties and the most heterogeneous interests. So improvements in cooperative capability may disproportionately help the broadest coalitions, because they're the ones most bottlenecked on it. The narrow harmful coalitions, like a cartel of three firms, often don't need much help; they can already coordinate.

A second consideration is that a lot of cooperative capabilities are also defensive. If I'm good at understanding other agents, I'm also better at detecting when others are colluding against me. Transparency, verification, credible commitment — these help the broader public resist exploitation as much as they help narrow groups coordinate. So it's not a one-sided weapon.

But I don't want to be too glib about it. I think the honest answer is that you have to look at specific capabilities and specific deployment contexts. Some capabilities, like better mechanisms for verifying commitments between states, seem pretty robustly good. Others, like tools that help agents coordinate in ways that are opaque to outsiders, seem more worrying. And part of the research agenda of Cooperative AI is exactly to differentiate those cases, rather than treating cooperation as a monolithic good.

So I'd summarise by saying: cooperation is not intrinsically good, it's instrumentally good conditional on the structure of the problem. And a big part of the job is to understand that structure well enough that we can steer the development of cooperative capabilities toward the cases where the externalities are positive, and toward the kinds of mechanisms — like transparency and broad inclusion — that make collusion against third parties harder rather than easier.

r001.rationale: The response says cooperative capabilities can be used for beneficial coordination or harmful collusion, depending on the situation, characterizing them as dual-use.

r002.rationale: It says that, on balance, increasing cooperative capability tends to be good, while noting that effects depend on the capabilities and deployment contexts.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: cooperation among whom, and to what end? Cooperation isn’t automatically socially beneficial. A group of companies could cooperate to improve safety, but they could also cooperate to exclude competitors or avoid accountability. So we need to distinguish benefits to the parties cooperating from benefits to society more broadly.

I’d look at the particular failures that greater cooperative skill would help us overcome. For example, if companies would all prefer to take more time to establish that their systems are safe, but each feels pressure to move quickly because the others might, then better communication, credible commitments, and verification could make everyone better off. And that could benefit people who aren’t represented in those negotiations.

But you also need to ask who bears the costs, whose interests are missing, and whether the arrangement can be challenged or revised. An agreement that’s stable and advantageous for its members could still be terrible for everyone else.

So my assessment would be conditional. I’d be enthusiastic about improving our ability to make and verify agreements that address shared risks. I’d be much less confident that simply making existing groups more effective at coordinating necessarily improves the world. The objective should be cooperation that serves broadly shared interests, with institutions that help keep it accountable to those interests.

r001.rationale: It describes cooperation as useful for safety and shared risks, but also as usable to exclude competitors or avoid accountability, framing the capability as dual-use.

r002.rationale: The response gives a conditional assessment and says that broadly improving coordination does not necessarily improve the world; it does not judge the increase probably beneficial on net.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: cooperation among whom, and towards what end? Increasing people’s ability to cooperate isn’t necessarily socially beneficial. A group of firms could become better at coordinating on safety standards, but they could also become better at excluding competitors or avoiding accountability. So we shouldn’t equate cooperation with doing good.

What I’d want to understand is which obstacles to cooperation are currently preventing socially beneficial outcomes. For example, perhaps firms would all prefer a world in which they take adequate time to evaluate dangerous systems, but each fears that slowing down will allow a competitor to get ahead. Better communication, monitoring, and credible commitments could help them achieve that outcome together.

But then you also have to ask who isn’t represented in that agreement. Do the benefits extend to the public, to other countries, and to future generations? Or are the participants simply getting better at advancing their own interests at everyone else’s expense?

So I’d assess particular cooperative capabilities in particular contexts, rather than assume that increasing cooperative skill across the ecosystem is uniformly good. The most promising cases are those where you can identify a shared problem, explain how improved cooperation helps solve it, and establish some accountability to the people affected.

r001.rationale: It describes improved cooperation as useful for coordinating on safety, but also for excluding competitors or avoiding accountability, clearly framing it as dual-use.

r002.rationale: It rejects assuming that increased cooperative skill across the ecosystem is uniformly good and makes no judgment that it is probably beneficial on net.
